Identify the grammatical error in the sentence below.

Amazon Prime Day is going to kick up the holiday season and holiday shopping for many consumers.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error in the sentence is the incorrect use of the phrasal verb "**kick up**."
 
• The intended meaning in this context is to start or commence the holiday season. The appropriate phrasal verb for this is "**kick off**."
 
• "**Kick off**" means to begin or start an event or a period of time (e.g., *The festival kicks off this Friday*).
 
• "**Kick up**" typically means to create something unpleasant, such as a fuss, trouble, or to stir up dust (e.g., *The wind kicked up a lot of dust*).

Therefore, the correct answer is **1**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"Amazon Prime Day is going to **kick off** the holiday season and holiday shopping for many consumers."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 2: "for many consumers"** – This prepositional phrase is used correctly to indicate the people affected by the shopping season.
 
• **Option 3: "up the holiday season"** – While this contains the incorrect particle "up," the primary grammatical error is rooted in the phrasal verb structure found in Option 1.
 
• **Option 4: "holiday season and holiday shopping"** – This compound direct object is grammatically correct and logically connected by the conjunction "and."
 
• **Usage Note:** Phrasal verbs are highly context-dependent. Always verify if the particle (up, off, on, out) aligns with the intended action of the base verb.

• **Reported Speech:** She told me that she had been learning French for three months.
 
• **Key Conversions:**
 
 
• **"She had been learning" becomes "I have been learning"**
 
 
• Indirect speech tense (past perfect continuous) is converted to direct speech tense (present perfect continuous).
 
• Pronoun "she" is changed to "I" for direct speech.
 
 
 
• **"French for three months" remains unchanged**

• **Reporting verb:**
 
 
• Indirect: "She told me"
 
• Converted to: "She said to me," which is appropriate for direct speech.
 
 
 
 
 
• **Punctuation and Format:**
 
 
• Direct speech is enclosed in quotation marks.
 
• Starts with a capital letter "I" and ends with a period ".".
 
• Reporting clause follows the quoted speech, separated by a comma.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"She said to me, "I have been learning French for three months.""*

questions.question:
Which is the correct verb tense used in the sentence:

"There has been a noticeable surge in gold prices..."
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**Option 3 (Present perfect)**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

__
 
• ***Option 1: Past simple***

 
 
• This is **incorrect**. Past simple would be “There was a noticeable surge,” but the sentence uses “has been,” which indicates continuity into the present.
 
 
 
• ***Option 2: Future perfect***
 
 
• This is **incorrect**. Future perfect would be “There will have been,” which refers to a completed action in the future, not the present.
 
 
 
• ***Option 3: Present perfect***
 
 
• This is **correct**. “Has been” is the present perfect tense, used to describe an action that began in the past and continues to have relevance or effect in the present.
 
 
 
• ***Option 4: Past continuous***
 
 
• This is **incorrect**. Past continuous would be “There was being a surge,” which is ungrammatical and does not match the sentence structure.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3 (Present perfect)**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** 

 
• **Present perfect tense** is formed with *has/have + past participle*.
 
• It is used to describe actions that started in the past but are still relevant or continuing in the present.
 
• Example: “She has lived here for five years.” → She started living in the past and continues to live here now.
 
• In the passage: “There has been a noticeable surge in gold prices” → The surge began earlier and is still relevant now.

questions.question: Which article of the Indian Constitution mentions that There shall be a Comptroller and Auditor-General of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 148**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 148** of the Indian Constitution mentions the establishment of the **Comptroller and Auditor-General (CAG) of India**.
 
• The CAG is responsible for auditing all receipts and expenditures of the Government of India and the state governments, including bodies and authorities substantially financed by the government.
 
• The CAG is considered the guardian of the public purse and ensures accountability and transparency in the financial administration of the country.
 
• The CAG is appointed by the **President of India** and holds office for a term of **6 years** or until attaining the age of **65 years**, whichever is earlier.
 
• Article 148 ensures the **independence of the CAG** by providing safeguards such as fixed tenure, removal procedure similar to that of a Supreme Court judge, and salary charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Role of the Comptroller and Auditor-General (CAG):**

 
 
• The CAG audits and reports on the accounts of the Union and State governments to ensure they are in compliance with laws and regulations.
 
• It examines whether expenditures were made for the intended purposes and whether the government’s financial transactions were conducted efficiently.
 
• The reports of the CAG are submitted to the **President of India** or the Governor of a state, who then table them in the respective legislature.
 
 
 
• **Constitutional Provisions:**
 
 
• **Articles 149-151** of the Indian Constitution further elaborate on the duties, powers, and responsibilities of the CAG.
 
• **Article 149:** Specifies the duties and powers of the CAG.
 
• **Article 150:** Provides that the accounts of the Union and the States shall be kept in the format prescribed by the President on the advice of the CAG.
 
• **Article 151:** Stipulates that the reports of the CAG on the accounts of the Union and the States shall be laid before the Parliament or the State Legislature.
 
 
 
• **Independence of the CAG:**
 
 
• The CAG is independent of the executive, and its authority is protected under the Constitution.
 
• Its salary and other conditions of service cannot be varied to its disadvantage after appointment.
 
• The CAG is removed from office in the same manner as a judge of the Supreme Court, which ensures its independence.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Reports by CAG:**
 
 
• The CAG has been instrumental in uncovering several financial irregularities, such as the **2G spectrum case** and the **coal allocation scam**.
 
• Such reports lead to corrective measures and reforms in governance.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Article 142:** Grants the Supreme Court the power to pass any decree or order necessary to ensure complete justice.
 
• **Article 144:** Mandates all authorities, civil and judicial, in India to act in aid of the Supreme Court.
 
• **Article 146:** Deals with the conditions of service of officers and employees of the Supreme Court.
 
• None of these articles pertain to the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, which is specifically covered under **Article 148**.

questions.question: Which section of the Indian constitution ensure social and economic reforms in a country?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Directive Principles of State Policy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• The **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)** are outlined in **Part IV** of the **Indian Constitution**, spanning from **Articles 36 to 51**. These principles serve as guidelines for the state to ensure **socio-economic reforms** and to establish a just society.

• The DPSP aim to promote **economic equality**, reduce the disparity between the rich and the poor, and provide for the welfare of citizens by ensuring access to resources, healthcare, education, and employment.

• These principles are **non-justiciable**, meaning they cannot be enforced by courts. However, they act as a guiding framework for the government to formulate laws and policies.

• Key provisions under DPSP include ensuring adequate means of livelihood, equitable distribution of wealth, equal pay for equal work, protection of children and youth, free legal aid, and promotion of education and public health.

• Some examples of socio-economic reforms influenced by DPSP include the implementation of the **Right to Education Act** (2009) and the establishment of schemes like **MGNREGA** and **National Food Security Act**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Fundamental Rights**: 

• These are outlined in **Part III** of the Indian Constitution and guarantee civil liberties to individuals, such as the **right to equality, freedom, and protection against exploitation**.

• They are **justiciable** and can be enforced through courts.

• Examples include **Article 14 (Right to Equality)** and **Article 21 (Right to Life and Personal Liberty)**.

• **Fundamental Duties**: 

• Added by the **42nd Amendment Act, 1976**, and listed under **Article 51A**, these duties are non-justiciable and act as moral obligations for citizens.

• Examples include respecting the Constitution, promoting harmony, and protecting the environment.

• **Separation of Powers**: 

• This principle ensures that the **legislative, executive, and judiciary** function independently to maintain a system of checks and balances.

• It is not explicitly mentioned in the Constitution but is derived from its provisions to prevent abuse of power.

• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)**:

• They are inspired by the **Irish Constitution** and aim to establish **economic democracy**.

• Some specific articles include:

• **Article 39(b):** Distribution of material resources to subserve the common good.

• **Article 41:** Right to work, education, and public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, or sickness.

• **Article 47:** Duty of the state to raise the level of nutrition and standard of living.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Relationship Between DPSP and Fundamental Rights**:

• While **Fundamental Rights** ensure individual freedoms, the **Directive Principles** focus on the collective welfare of society.

• In cases of conflict, courts have attempted to harmonize both. For instance, the **Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973)** established that DPSPs cannot override Fundamental Rights but play a crucial role in governance.

• **Implementation Challenges**:

• The non-justiciable nature of DPSP makes their enforcement dependent on the political will of the government.

• The **Battle of Plassey** took place on **23 June 1757** between the forces of the British East India Company led by **Robert Clive** and the Nawab of Bengal, **Siraj-ud-Daulah**. 
• The battle was fought near **Plassey**, located in present-day **West Bengal**, along the banks of the Bhagirathi River. 
• The British East India Company secured a decisive victory due to the betrayal by **Mir Jafar**, the commander of Siraj-ud-Daulah's army, who sided with the British. 
• This victory marked the beginning of **British political dominance** in India, as it paved the way for the establishment of British control over Bengal and later other parts of India. 
• The **Battle of Plassey** is widely regarded as the **first major victory** of the British East India Company in India, setting the foundation for their empire in the subcontinent. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• It was a significant victory for the British, leading to the end of French ambitions in India. However, this occurred after the Battle of Plassey.

• **Robert Clive:** 
• Robert Clive, often called "Clive of India," was the British commander who led the forces during the Battle of Plassey. 
• He played a crucial role in establishing British supremacy in India. 
• **Mir Jafar:** 
• Mir Jafar's betrayal of Siraj-ud-Daulah was instrumental in the British victory at Plassey. 
• He was later installed as the Nawab of Bengal but remained under British influence. 
• **Economic Impact:** 
• The victory at Plassey provided the British East India Company access to Bengal's **resources**, including its lucrative **trade routes** and **wealth**.

questions.question: Which bill/act provided for the trial of British or European persons by Indians, and sought equality between British and Indian judges?

 __ 
• The **Ilbert Bill** was introduced in **1883** by **Sir Courtenay Ilbert**, the Law Member of the Viceroy's Council during the tenure of **Lord Ripon**, the then Viceroy of India. 
• This bill proposed to allow **Indian judges** to preside over cases involving British and other European subjects in India, ensuring **judicial equality**. 
• The bill aimed to **abolish racial discrimination** in the Indian judicial system and was a major step toward **legal equality** between Indians and Europeans. 
• However, the bill faced **strong opposition** from the European community in India, who saw it as a threat to their privileged position. 
• Due to the backlash, the bill was **amended**, which led to a compromise. The amended version allowed European subjects to request a jury with at least half of its members being Europeans. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Background of the Ilbert Bill:** 
• Before the Ilbert Bill, the judicial system in India was **highly biased**, with British subjects being tried only by British judges. 
• The bill was part of Lord Ripon’s broader vision of **liberal reforms** and efforts to grant Indians more authority in governance. 
• **Impact of Opposition:** 
• The opposition to the Ilbert Bill highlighted the **deep-seated racial prejudices** among the European settlers in India. 
• The agitation against the bill reinforced the divide between Indians and Europeans, leading to a **greater nationalistic awakening** among Indians. 
• **Lord Ripon’s Legacy:** 
• Lord Ripon is remembered as the **“Father of Local Self-Government in India”** for his efforts to empower Indians in administrative roles. 
• Other notable reforms during his tenure include the **reduction of press restrictions** and the introduction of local self-governance. 
• **Significance of the Ilbert Bill:** 
• The Ilbert Bill controversy was a pivotal moment in Indian history, as it **exposed the discriminatory policies** of the British and inspired early nationalist movements. 
• It also encouraged Indians to **fight for equality and self-governance** through organized efforts. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Regulating Act of 1773:** 
• This act established the **Supreme Court of Judicature** in Calcutta and marked the beginning of the British judiciary in India. 
• It did not address the issue of judicial equality between Indians and Europeans. 
• **Pitt’s India Act of 1784:** 
• This act primarily dealt with the **administrative control** of the East India Company and did not involve judicial reforms. 
• **Indian Councils Act of 1892:** 
• This act was aimed at expanding the **legislative councils** and increasing Indian participation in governance but had no relevance to judicial matters.

questions.question: In 1991, rupee was devalued in two stages and the cumulative devaluation was about ___________ percent in USD terms.

__

• In **1991**, the Indian rupee was devalued in two stages to address the **severe balance of payments (BoP) crisis**.

• The cumulative devaluation of the rupee was approximately **18 percent in USD terms**. This was undertaken to stabilize the economy.

• The devaluation was implemented under the leadership of then **Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao** and **Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh**.

• The move was part of a broader economic reform package aimed at liberalizing the Indian economy and moving towards a **market-driven exchange rate system**.

• This decision was crucial in restoring investor confidence and attracting foreign capital, thereby averting a financial crisis.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Background of the 1991 Economic Crisis:**

• India faced a **severe BoP crisis** in 1991 due to dwindling foreign exchange reserves, rising imports, and falling exports.

• Foreign reserves were so low that they could barely cover **three weeks of imports**.

• The Gulf War of 1990–1991 aggravated the crisis by increasing **oil prices** and reducing remittances from Indian workers in the Gulf region.

• **Steps Taken During the Crisis:**

• India secured loans from the **International Monetary Fund (IMF)**, but these were conditional on implementing structural reforms.

• The government initiated the **Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization (LPG)** reforms to open up the economy.

• The devaluation of the rupee was a key measure to make Indian exports more competitive and reduce the trade deficit.

• **Impact of the Rupee Devaluation:**

• The devaluation boosted **exports** by making Indian goods cheaper in international markets.

• It helped in **stabilizing foreign reserves** and restoring macroeconomic stability.

• The move also paved the way for long-term economic reforms, transforming India into a **market-driven economy**.

• **Key Figures Behind the Reforms:**

• **P.V. Narasimha Rao:** As the Prime Minister, he spearheaded the economic reforms and provided political backing.

• **Dr. Manmohan Singh:** As the Finance Minister, he played a pivotal role in formulating and implementing the reforms.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Devaluation Process:**

• The first stage of devaluation occurred on **July 1, 1991**, when the rupee was devalued by approximately **9 percent**.

• The second stage followed on **July 3, 1991**, with an additional devaluation of around **9 percent**.

• **Exchange Rate Changes:**

• Before devaluation, the exchange rate was approximately **17.90 INR/USD**.

• After the devaluation, it increased to around **23 INR/USD**, reflecting an 18 percent cumulative change.

• **IMF Loan Conditions:**

• The devaluation was a precondition for receiving financial assistance from the **IMF**.

• Other conditions included **fiscal discipline**, reduction in subsidies, and promotion of foreign investment.

questions.question: Which of the following Indian states does not have a Legislative Council?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rajasthan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Legislative Council** is the upper house in states with a bicameral legislature, while the Legislative Assembly is the lower house.

• Currently, only **six Indian states** have a Legislative Council: **Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Karnataka.**

• **Rajasthan** does not have a Legislative Council and follows a unicameral legislative system, with only a Legislative Assembly.

• The Legislative Councils in states are established under **Article 169** of the Indian Constitution.

• Creating or abolishing a Legislative Council requires a resolution passed by the Legislative Assembly of the state, followed by a parliamentary approval.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Legislative Council in India:** 

• The Legislative Council is also known as the **Vidhan Parishad**, and its members are called MLCs (**Members of Legislative Council**).

• The members of the Council are elected, nominated, or appointed through various methods such as elections by Legislative Assembly members, graduates, teachers, and local authorities.

• It serves as a revising chamber for bills passed by the Legislative Assembly and also provides expertise on policy matters.

• **Unicameral and Bicameral Legislature:** 

• **Unicameral legislature** refers to states with only one legislative body, the Legislative Assembly.

• **Bicameral legislature** includes states with two houses: the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council.

• Examples of bicameral states include **Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, and Maharashtra**, while states like **Rajasthan** follow a unicameral structure.

• **Article 169 of the Indian Constitution:** 

• This article provides the procedure for creating or abolishing the Legislative Council in a state.

• A state assembly must pass a resolution by a **special majority** (two-thirds of members present and voting) to initiate this process.

• The Parliament then enacts a law for the creation or abolition of the Legislative Council.

• **Historical Context:** 

• Initially, several states like Rajasthan, Punjab, and West Bengal had Legislative Councils, but they were later abolished due to financial and administrative concerns.

• The abolition of Legislative Councils is often debated due to concerns over their **effectiveness and necessity.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Structure of State Legislature:** 

• The Constitution of India allows states to choose between a unicameral and bicameral legislative system.

• States with a unicameral system only have a Legislative Assembly, which handles law-making and governance.

• Bicameral states have an additional house, the Legislative Council, which functions similarly to the Rajya Sabha at the national level.

• **Advantages of Legislative Council:** 

• Provides a platform for experienced individuals to contribute to law-making without contesting elections.

• Serves as a check and balance mechanism for bills passed by the Legislative Assembly.

• Facilitates representation for specific groups such as teachers and graduates.

• **Disadvantages of Legislative Council:** 

• Often criticized for being redundant and delaying legislative processes.

• Involves additional financial burdens on the state government.

• Its necessity and functionality are debated, especially in states with limited financial resources.

questions.question:
Which of the following statement is correct regarding the article 253 of Indian Constitution?

I. It is found in Part XI of the Constitution.

II. It relates to the Legislation for giving effect to international agreements.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both I and II**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Article 253** of the **Indian Constitution** is located in **Part XI**, which deals with the **relations between the Union and the States**. *Hence, statement I is correct.* 
• It empowers **Parliament** to make laws for the entire country or any part of it to implement **international treaties, agreements, or conventions**. *Hence, statement II is correct.* 
• This article allows the Parliament to legislate even on subjects in the **State List**, if required to fulfill international obligations. 
• The legislative power under Article 253 is derived from the principle of **federal flexibility** in India’s Constitution. 
• Examples include laws made to fulfill obligations under **international agreements** like the **UNFCCC (United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change)** or treaties related to human rights. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Part XI of the Indian Constitution:** 
• Part XI deals with the **distribution of legislative and administrative powers** between the Union and the States. 
• It includes Articles **245 to 263**, covering topics such as the extent of laws made by Parliament and state legislatures and coordination between the Union and States. 
• Article 253 is located within this part and highlights the flexibility of legislative powers for international obligations. 
• **International Treaties and Agreements:** 
• India, as a signatory to several **international conventions**, requires domestic laws to ensure compliance. 
• Examples include the **Environmental Protection Act** (1986) implemented to fulfill obligations under **international environmental agreements**. 
• Parliament can make laws on subjects in the **State List** to meet these obligations under Article 253. 
• **Federal Flexibility:** 
• The Indian Constitution is characterized by a strong center, allowing the Union Parliament to legislate on subjects normally reserved for states in certain situations. 
• Such flexibility ensures effective governance and compliance with **international obligations**. 
• **Important Examples:** 
• The **Protection of Human Rights Act**, enacted to comply with **international human rights treaties**. 
• Legislation related to climate change like the **Energy Conservation Act** aligns with global agreements like the **Paris Agreement**. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Legislative Competence:** 
• Under Article 253, Parliament holds the authority to legislate on **any subject**, including those under the State List, to give effect to international agreements. 
• This does not require prior approval from state legislatures, showcasing India’s **unitary tilt** in certain aspects of federalism. 
• **Key Examples:** 
• The **Atomic Energy Act** (1962) was enacted to fulfill obligations under international treaties concerning the peaceful use of atomic energy. 
• The **Foreign Trade Act** (1992) was implemented in response to global trade agreements. 
• **Judicial Interpretation:** 
• Indian courts have upheld the legislative power of Parliament under Article 253 in cases like **Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel v. Union of India** (1969). 
• This reinforces the principle that Parliament can legislate on state subjects to fulfill international obligations.
